nodes.title: Splunk SPL (Splunk Core Certified User/Power User): Key Ideas
nodes.content: SPL (Search Processing Language) is Splunk's query language. The Splunk Core exam tests the search pipeline, statistical commands (`stats`, `chart`, `timechart`), field extraction with `rex`, deduplication, transaction grouping, and lookup enrichment — all composable in a left-to-right pipe syntax.

flashcards.front: What is the SPL search pipeline?
flashcards.back: SPL is a sequence of commands separated by `|`. Results flow left to right: each command transforms the output of the previous. Example: `index=web status=404 | stats count by uri | sort -count | head 10`. The first segment (before the first `|`) is the search command that retrieves events from the index; subsequent pipes refine, aggregate, or format those events.

flashcards.front: stats vs chart vs timechart — what does each produce?
flashcards.back: `stats`: aggregate over all results into a flat table — `stats count, avg(bytes) by status`. `chart`: produce a table with one row per value of the BY clause and columns per OVER clause — good for cross-tabulations. `timechart`: time-bucketed aggregation with _time on the X-axis — `timechart span=1h avg(response_ms) by host`. Use timechart for trend charts in dashboards.

flashcards.front: What does `rex` do and when do you need it?
flashcards.back: `rex` extracts fields using a named capture group regex inline during search — e.g., `rex field=_raw "user=(?<username>\w+)"` creates a `username` field without modifying the source data. Use it when a field you need isn't already extracted by a field extraction (props.conf/transforms.conf). For permanent extraction, define it in transforms.conf; for ad-hoc exploration, use `rex`.

flashcards.front: transaction vs stats — when do you use transaction?
flashcards.back: `transaction` groups related events into a single event based on shared field values and/or time gaps — e.g., `transaction session_id maxspan=30m` groups all web events for the same session. It preserves raw event content and adds `duration` and `eventcount` fields. Use it when you need the full raw events; use `stats` when you only need aggregated values — `stats` is orders of magnitude faster at scale.

nodes.title: Splunk knowledge objects (Splunk Core): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Knowledge objects are the building blocks of Splunk data enrichment: field aliases rename existing fields, calculated fields derive new ones, event types classify events, tags add metadata, macros define reusable search snippets, and data models power Pivot and Accelerated search. The Core exam tests what each object does and the order in which Splunk applies them.

flashcards.front: Field alias vs calculated field — what is the difference?
flashcards.back: Field alias: creates an alternate name for an existing extracted field — `clientip` aliased as `src_ip`. No data is duplicated; both names point to the same value. Calculated field: creates a brand-new field whose value is derived by an `eval` expression — `response_kb = bytes / 1024`. Calculated fields require the source field(s) to already exist; they add a derived column.

flashcards.front: Event types vs tags — how do they differ?
flashcards.back: Event type: a saved search that classifies events matching its criteria — e.g., `index=web status>=400` is the `http_errors` event type. Any event matching it gets the `eventtype=http_errors` field. Tags: user-defined labels attached to specific field=value pairs — e.g., tag the value `status=404` with the tag `not_found`. Tags and event types both enrich events; event types are search-based classification, tags are value-based labeling.

flashcards.front: Macros — what problem do they solve?
flashcards.back: Macros are saved SPL snippets (optionally with arguments) that can be referenced in any search using backtick syntax: `` `web_errors` `` expands to the full search string defined in the macro. They solve DRY violations — if your team writes the same 40-character filter in 50 searches, a macro means you change it in one place. Arguments (`macro(arg1,arg2)`) make macros reusable across different index names, timeframes, etc.

flashcards.front: Data models and CIM — what is each?
flashcards.back: Data model: a hierarchical schema that describes the expected fields and constraints for a type of data (Web, Network Traffic, Authentication) — the foundation for Pivot UI and accelerated searches. CIM (Common Information Model): Splunk's standard data model library with normalized field names across data sources — `src_ip`, `dest_ip`, `action` instead of vendor-specific names. CIM compliance means every app speaks the same field language, enabling cross-source correlation.

questions.q: An analyst wants to enrich search results with data from an external CSV `asset_owners.csv`, joining on a key field, and also to list the CSV contents directly. Which pair of features fits?
choices: A lookup definition for the enrichment; `inputlookup` to load CSV rows into the pipeline
A field alias for the enrichment; `metadata` command to list the CSV rows
An event type for the enrichment; `outputlookup` to load CSV rows into the pipeline
A tag for the enrichment; `dbxquery` to load CSV rows into the pipeline
questions.explanation: Lookups enrich events with external data (CSV, KV Store, geo, DB) by matching a key. `inputlookup <table>` reads the lookup table into the pipeline as rows. A field alias (A) just renames existing fields, not an enrichment; `metadata` inspects indexes, not lookup files. An event type (C) categorises events by search, not by external data; `outputlookup` writes to a lookup, not reads. Tags (D) label field=value pairs; `dbxquery` is the DB Connect app's SQL runner, not a CSV reader.

questions.q: An automatic lookup is configured in `Settings → Lookups → Automatic Lookups`. What does it do?
choices: Refreshes the underlying CSV file from an external source on the lookup's own schedule
Applies the lookup silently to searches whose events contain the input field
Writes new rows into the lookup file automatically when events introduce new key values
Forwards lookup output back to the indexers to be re-ingested as new indexed events
questions.explanation: An automatic lookup silently applies the mapping at search time whenever an event contains the lookup's input field — no `| lookup` needed in the SPL. Option A confuses automatic lookups with KV Store collection refresh or a scheduled `outputlookup` job. Option C is wrong — lookups are read-only from the search side; new rows require an explicit `outputlookup`. Option D is not a Splunk feature at all.

questions.q: An admin wants `clientip` to also be queryable as `src_ip` so legacy dashboards keep working. Which knowledge object provides this at search time?
choices: Calculated field — computes a new value from an eval expression
Event type — categorises events by a saved search
Field alias — maps one field name to another at search time
Tag — labels a specific field=value pair
questions.explanation: A field alias (`Settings → Fields → Field Aliases`) creates an alternative name for an existing field, applied per source type at search time. Event types (B) categorise events matching a search — they add an `eventtype` value, not a field alias. Calculated fields (C) run an `eval` to derive a new value; they do not create name aliases. Tags (D) label specific `field=value` pairs, not fields themselves.

questions.q: A SOC wants to categorise events at search time via a saved search expression (e.g. `index=fw action=blocked` → `firewall_deny`). Which knowledge object does this?
choices: Tag — labels field values, not events matching a search
Event type — a saved search expression that categorises matching events
Field extraction — pulls new fields from raw text, not categorisation
Workflow action — a right-click UI link, not a saved category
questions.explanation: An event type is a saved search that categorises any matching event by attaching an `eventtype` value. Tags (A) label individual field=value pairs and are commonly applied ON TOP of event types, but they do not use a search expression themselves. Field extractions (C) generate new fields from raw text. Workflow actions (D) are UI-level click-throughs from a field value to an external system.

questions.q: Tags and event types are related knowledge objects. Which correctly describes both?
choices: Tags apply system-wide always; event types only apply within a single dashboard panel
Tags apply at index-time only; event types apply at search-time only, never earlier
Tags label specific field=value pairs; event types categorise events by a saved search
Tags depend on a CSV lookup file; event types depend on a KV Store collection to work
questions.explanation: A tag is a label attached to a specific `field=value` pair (e.g. tagging `sourcetype=access_combined` with 'web'). An event type is a categorisation saved as a search — matching events pick up an `eventtype` value. Tags may then be applied to event types. Option B is wrong — both are search-time constructs. Option A is invented. Option D confuses them with lookup / KV Store enrichment, which is a separate mechanism.

questions.q: Splunk knowledge-object sharing has three scopes: Private, App, and Global. Which describes App vs Global correctly?
choices: App = visible to all users of a specific app; Global = visible across every app
App = visible only to the object's creator; Global = visible to their role peers
App and Global are synonyms — both make the object visible everywhere in Splunk
App = objects manageable via REST only; Global = objects manageable via UI only
questions.explanation: Private means only the creator sees the object. App restricts visibility to users of a specific app (`search`, `enterprise_security`, etc.). Global exposes the object across every app to anyone with the required role. Option B conflates them. Option C inverts the meanings. Option D confuses sharing scope with the transport used to manage the object.

questions.q: An admin defines `EVAL-response_ms = response_ns / 1000000` in `props.conf` so every matching event gains the field at search time — no data rewrite. Which feature is this?
choices: Calculated field
Index-time field extraction — modifies data during indexing
Field alias — renames an existing field
Automatic lookup — enriches from an external table
questions.explanation: A calculated field applies an `eval` expression at search time to every event of a matching sourcetype, without touching indexed data. Option B is wrong — the point of a calculated field is that it runs at SEARCH time, not index time. Option C only renames a field, it does not compute. Option D reads from an external table (CSV / KV Store), which is not what a plain `eval` expression does.

questions.q: Two ways to define a field extraction in Splunk: inline `EXTRACT-<name>` in `props.conf`, and `TRANSFORMS-<class>` pointing to a stanza in `transforms.conf`. Which describes the pair correctly?
choices: Both run at index-time; they differ only in file location and stanza naming
Inline is search-time; TRANSFORMS unlocks SOURCE_KEY, FORMAT, MV_ADD, REPEAT_MATCH
Inline runs at search-time; TRANSFORMS runs at index-time only
Inline is defined via the `rex` SPL command; TRANSFORMS uses the `erex` command
questions.explanation: Both live at search time. Inline `EXTRACT-` is compact — one regex per stanza in `props.conf`. `TRANSFORMS-<class>` in `props.conf` references a stanza in `transforms.conf` (via `REGEX` / `FORMAT`) and unlocks features like `SOURCE_KEY`, format templates, `MV_ADD`, and `REPEAT_MATCH`. Option A is wrong — neither is index-time. Option C reverses the truth. Option D confuses `.conf` extractions with SPL commands.

nodes.title: Ingest: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Ingest. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: An admin wants Splunk to tail `/var/log/auth.log` on a Linux host and forward new lines to the indexer. Which input type in `inputs.conf` is correct?
flashcards.back: `[monitor://path]` is the file-tailing input, typically deployed via a Universal Forwarder. `[tcp://...]` (B) receives network senders (syslog, etc.); it doesn't watch a local file. HEC (C) is an HTTP-POST endpoint for apps — the stanza syntax shown is wrong anyway (HEC is configured via `inputs.conf` `[http]` plus tokens, not a URL). Scripted inputs (D) execute a script on a schedule; useful for data a script generates, not for tailing a log file.

flashcards.front: An app team wants to push events to Splunk over HTTPS with a token — no forwarder installed. Which Splunk feature enables this?
flashcards.back: HEC receives JSON events over HTTPS at `/services/collector` using token authentication — no forwarder needed. Option B is a REST endpoint for managing saved searches, not ingesting events. Option C is fictional — the UF is by definition an agent. Option D is the port indexers use to receive forwarder traffic; it is not a general app-ingest API and requires forwarder framing.

flashcards.front: An ingest stanza sets no `sourcetype`. How does Splunk decide the sourcetype at index time?
flashcards.back: Splunk's automatic source typing uses filename patterns via `[source::...]` stanzas, built-in rules for common formats (CSV, JSON, syslog, Apache), and content-analysis fallbacks (`_json`, `_xml`, `generic_single_line`). Option A is wrong — UFs do not blanket-assign `syslog`. Option C confuses sourcetype with index; they are independent. Option D is not a real fallback name in Splunk.

flashcards.front: Splunk extracts fields in two architectural stages: index-time and search-time. Which describes the trade-off correctly?
flashcards.back: Index-time bakes values into the index — searches are faster but storage grows and mistakes are baked in. Search-time regex runs per query, saving storage at CPU cost, and can be edited without re-indexing. Splunk recommends search-time for almost all cases. Option A denies the whole architectural distinction. Option B swaps the tiers backwards. Option D is wrong — search-time extractions ARE regex-based.

questions.q: An admin wants Splunk to tail `/var/log/auth.log` on a Linux host and forward new lines to the indexer. Which input type in `inputs.conf` is correct?
choices: Scripted input: `[script:///opt/scripts/tail.sh]`
TCP input: `[tcp://514]`
HTTP Event Collector: `[http://splunk:8088]`
File monitor input: `[monitor:///var/log/auth.log]`
questions.explanation: `[monitor://path]` is the file-tailing input, typically deployed via a Universal Forwarder. `[tcp://...]` (B) receives network senders (syslog, etc.); it doesn't watch a local file. HEC (C) is an HTTP-POST endpoint for apps — the stanza syntax shown is wrong anyway (HEC is configured via `inputs.conf` `[http]` plus tokens, not a URL). Scripted inputs (D) execute a script on a schedule; useful for data a script generates, not for tailing a log file.

questions.q: An app team wants to push events to Splunk over HTTPS with a token — no forwarder installed. Which Splunk feature enables this?
choices: HTTP Event Collector (HEC) — POST to `/services/collector` with a token
REST API `saved/searches` — used for saved-search management, not raw ingest
Universal Forwarder in agentless mode — no such agentless mode exists
TCP input on port 9997 — indexer replication port, not a public app-ingest path
questions.explanation: HEC receives JSON events over HTTPS at `/services/collector` using token authentication — no forwarder needed. Option B is a REST endpoint for managing saved searches, not ingesting events. Option C is fictional — the UF is by definition an agent. Option D is the port indexers use to receive forwarder traffic; it is not a general app-ingest API and requires forwarder framing.

questions.q: An ingest stanza sets no `sourcetype`. How does Splunk decide the sourcetype at index time?
choices: The Universal Forwarder always sets it to `syslog`
Automatic source typing
It inherits the value of the target index
It is always tagged `unknown` until manually re-assigned
questions.explanation: Splunk's automatic source typing uses filename patterns via `[source::...]` stanzas, built-in rules for common formats (CSV, JSON, syslog, Apache), and content-analysis fallbacks (`_json`, `_xml`, `generic_single_line`). Option A is wrong — UFs do not blanket-assign `syslog`. Option C confuses sourcetype with index; they are independent. Option D is not a real fallback name in Splunk.

questions.q: Splunk extracts fields in two architectural stages: index-time and search-time. Which describes the trade-off correctly?
choices: Both perform equivalently; the distinction is only a documentation label used by Splunk trainers
Index-time runs on the search head at query time; search-time runs on indexers during ingest
Index-time stores fields in the index (fast search, bigger storage); search-time extracts on demand
Index-time is regex-based; search-time only supports key=value pair auto-extraction
questions.explanation: Index-time bakes values into the index — searches are faster but storage grows and mistakes are baked in. Search-time regex runs per query, saving storage at CPU cost, and can be edited without re-indexing. Splunk recommends search-time for almost all cases. Option A denies the whole architectural distinction. Option B swaps the tiers backwards. Option D is wrong — search-time extractions ARE regex-based.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An admin sets up an alert: 'fire when the count of failed logins from a single IP exceeds 10 in any 15-minute window' using `stats count by src_ip | where count > 10`. Which trigger-condition setting fits?
choices: Number of events > 10 — counts raw events, not the aggregated rows
Number of sources > 0 — 'sources' means `source` field, not result rows
Number of hosts > 10 — wrong dimension (hosts, not src_ip rows)
Number of results > 0 — fires whenever a row survives `where count > 10`
questions.explanation: Because the search transforms events into a per-src_ip table and pre-filters with `where count > 10`, ANY row that survives is already a violation — so the alert trigger 'Number of results > 0' fires exactly when needed. Option A operates on raw event count, ignoring aggregation. Options C and D bind the trigger to unrelated dimensions (`host`, `source`) that have nothing to do with unique IPs above threshold.

questions.q: An alert fires on every 5-minute schedule and spams the ops team. The admin enables `throttle: suppress for 1 hour by src_ip`. What does throttling do?
choices: Suppresses re-firing of the alert for a time window, optionally per field value
Reduces the alert search's cron frequency
Limits the number of result rows via `head`-style truncation
Delays the initial trigger until a minimum number of matches accumulate
questions.explanation: Throttling prevents an alert from re-firing for a configured window after it fires, optionally scoped to a field value (so alerts are per-src_ip). This is the standard remedy for alert fatigue on persistent conditions. Option B changes schedule cadence, not throttling. Option C caps result rows, unrelated to firing. Option D describes the trigger threshold itself (e.g. 'number of results > N'), not throttling.

questions.q: Splunk alerts have two scheduling modes: real-time and scheduled. Which describes them correctly?
choices: Real-time = continuous rolling-window (timely, heavy); scheduled = runs on cron
Real-time alerts fire every one second regardless of the rolling-window size chosen
Real-time uses streaming-only evaluation on new events; scheduled evaluates historical data only
Real-time supports email delivery only; scheduled alerts are the only ones with all action types
questions.explanation: A real-time alert continuously evaluates a rolling window (e.g. the last 5 minutes) — most timely, most resource-heavy. Scheduled alerts run the search on a cron cadence and evaluate results after each completion. Option C is wrong — scheduled alerts can search any window including near-real-time. Option B invents a fixed 1-second cadence. Option D limits real-time to email, which is false.

questions.q: A team needs 3 years of monthly firewall aggregates without storing 3 years of raw events. Nightly, a search aggregates the day's events and writes summary rows to a dedicated index. Which technique is this?
choices: Bucket freezing — moves cold buckets off to slow storage
Report acceleration — pre-builds summaries on the original data
Data-model acceleration — builds tsidx summaries for a data model
Summary indexing
questions.explanation: Summary indexing uses `collect` (or `sistats`/`sichart`) to append aggregated rows to a summary index, so dashboards read a small pre-computed dataset. Report acceleration (B) speeds up ONE report by pre-computing partial results — it does not free you from retaining raw data. Data-model acceleration (C) accelerates data-model queries via tsidx summaries but still relies on raw retention. Bucket freezing (D) is retention lifecycle management, not aggregation.

questions.q: An analyst searches for HTTP requests where the URL contains `/admin`. Which SPL pattern is MOST efficient?
choices: `index=web | rex "/admin"` — `rex` extracts fields, doesn't filter
`index=web | regex url="/admin"` — post-process regex on every event
`index=web | eval m=if(match(url,"/admin"),1,0) | where m=1` — heavier still
`index=web url=*admin*` — indexed wildcard match in the initial search
questions.explanation: Putting the wildcard match in the initial search clause lets Splunk push the filter to the indexer's lispy engine (bloom filters + bucket elimination). Option B runs `regex` on every event AFTER retrieval, much slower. Option C is even worse — two passes over each event. Option A confuses `rex` (field extraction) with a filter — `rex` doesn't drop non-matching events at all.

questions.q: Splunk supports report acceleration: a saved report is registered and Splunk pre-computes partial summaries. Subsequent runs read those summaries. Which describes report acceleration correctly?
choices: Pre-computes partial summaries on disk; report must be transforming and scheduled
Report is transpiled into a native binary each night; subsequent runs execute the compiled artefact instead of SPL
Reads accelerated CIM data models directly via `tstats`, bypassing the report definition
Report caches results in RAM for one hour after each run; subsequent runs within that window return instantly
questions.explanation: Report acceleration continuously builds partial summaries on disk for a registered report; future runs read the summaries and only touch raw data for the recent uncovered window. Requirements: the report contains a transforming command, and it runs at least daily. Option D confuses it with a short-lived RAM cache. Option B invents JIT compilation. Option C describes data-model acceleration, which is a different feature — report acceleration is per-report.

questions.q: A dashboard panel must show event count by sourcetype over the last 24 hours and auto-refresh every 5 minutes. The team prefers relative-time historical searches over real-time. Which approach fits?
choices: A real-time 24-hour window with a 5-minute refresh — expensive and unnecessary
A one-off ad-hoc search re-run manually by the user
A historical search with `earliest=-24h latest=now` and a 5-minute panel refresh
A summary-indexing job that writes to `main` every minute
questions.explanation: Historical relative-time searches (`earliest=-24h latest=now`) plus a 5-minute panel auto-refresh give a rolling 24-hour view at low cost. Option A uses real-time, which continuously evaluates and is resource-intensive — the opposite of the requirement. Option B is not a solution, just manual reruns. Option D pollutes `main` (never write summary data there) and is far heavier than needed for a simple 24-hour panel.

questions.q: A dashboard exposes a text input where users type a hostname. The panel search uses `index=main host=$host_input$`. The `$...$` placeholder is a dashboard-level variable that updates panels when changed. What is this variable called?
choices: HEC token — authentication token for HTTP Event Collector
Token — dashboard variable referenced with `$name$`
REST API key — credential for `splunkd` REST endpoints
Session cookie — browser-side login state
questions.explanation: Splunk dashboards use TOKENS as the variable primitive: inputs set them, panel searches read them via `$token$`. Option A is an unrelated auth token used to POST events to HEC. Option C is a per-user credential for the REST API. Option D is browser state, not a dashboard variable. Only 'token' names the correct concept.
